facts.statehood_note: After seceding in 1861 and joining the Confederacy, Mississippi was restored to the Union on February 23, 1870, during Reconstruction.
facts.motto: Virtute et armis (Latin: By valor and arms)

symbols.name: Prehistoric whales (Basilosaurus cetoides and Zygorhiza kochii)

facts.name_origin: Named for the Mississippi River, which forms much of its western border. The river's name comes from the Ojibwe word misi-ziibi, meaning 'great river.'

government.chambers: Mississippi State Senate (52 members) and Mississippi House of Representatives (122 members); all serve four-year terms with no term limits
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; a person may be elected governor no more than twice). The lieutenant governor is elected on a separate ballot, and many department heads are also elected.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Mississippi (9 justices), elected in nonpartisan races from three districts to eight-year terms; the most senior justice serves as chief justice.
government.local: 82 counties, each run by an elected five-member Board of Supervisors.
government.constitution: The current constitution was adopted in 1890. White lawmakers wrote it to take voting power away from Black Mississippians, and about 100,000 Black and 50,000 white men were removed from the voter rolls; federal civil rights laws in 1964 and 1965 later restored voting rights. Earlier constitutions included the 1868 Reconstruction constitution, written by Black and white delegates.
government.kid_line: "All political power is vested in, and derived from, the people." (Article 3, Section 5)

long_ago.about: The Choctaw held large homelands in what is now Mississippi. Nanih Waiya, a mound and cave, is their sacred 'mother mound'; the Mississippi Band of Choctaw regained care of it in 2008.
The Chickasaw homelands were in northern Mississippi and nearby Alabama, Tennessee, and Kentucky. Their migration story tells of moving from west of the Mississippi River to northeast Mississippi.
The Natchez lived on the Natchez Bluffs along the lower Mississippi River and spoke a language with no known relatives. They used the Grand Village mound site in the 1600s and 1700s.
Beginning around 950 CE, Mississippian peoples farmed, traded from the Great Lakes to the Gulf Coast, and built large earthwork mounds; the Choctaw and Chickasaw descend from this culture.
Smaller nations such as the Biloxi and the Yazoo also lived in Mississippi; the city of Biloxi and the Yazoo River carry their names.

today.about: The only federally recognized tribe in Mississippi, organized in 1945, with reservation lands in Neshoba, Leake, Newton, Scott, Jones, Attala, Kemper, and Winston counties.

first_peoples.today_note: Most Choctaw and Chickasaw people were forced to move to Indian Territory (now Oklahoma) in the 1830s; the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and the Chickasaw Nation are based there today. Choctaw families who stayed in Mississippi under the 1830 treaty are ancestors of the Mississippi Band of Choctaw.
sites: Emerald Mound, Natchez Trace Parkway near Natchez, the second-largest Mississippian ceremonial mound in the United States, built and used from about 1200 to 1730 CE
Grand Village of the Natchez, Natchez, a village and three platform mounds begun about 1200 CE and later used by the Natchez people
Nanih Waiya, Winston County, the Choctaw 'mother mound,' cared for by the Mississippi Band of Choctaw since 2008

history.event: The first peoples (Paleo-Indian hunters) arrive in the South, hunting large Ice Age animals.
Mississippian peoples begin building large mounds and farming towns along the rivers.
Emerald Mound near Natchez is built and used; it covers eight acres.
French colonists build Fort Maurepas (Old Biloxi) near today's Ocean Springs, the first European settlement in Mississippi.
The French found Fort Rosalie at Natchez. French and Spanish colonists bring enslaved Africans to work on plantations.
In the Natchez War, the Natchez people rise up against French colonists; in revenge the French kill or deport most of the Natchez.
The United States creates the Mississippi Territory.
On December 10, Mississippi becomes the 20th state.

Under heavy pressure from settlers and the Indian Removal Act, Choctaw leaders sign the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, giving up about 11 million acres; most Choctaw are forced west on the Trail of Tears.
The Chickasaw are forced to sell their homelands in the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek and move to Indian Territory.
Mississippi is the nation's top cotton producer, built on the forced labor of 436,631 enslaved people, 55 percent of everyone in the state.

Mississippi secedes on January 9, 1861. Union forces besiege Vicksburg from May 18 to July 4, 1863, and win control of the Mississippi River; about 17,000 Black Mississippians serve in the Union Army.

A constitutional convention with 17 Black delegates out of 100 writes a constitution that adopts universal suffrage, ends property requirements for voting, and creates the state's first public school system. In 1870 Hiram Revels becomes the first African American in the U.S. Congress, and Mississippi rejoins the Union.
In the violent 'white line' campaign, armed white groups attack and kill Black voters and leaders, and Democrats retake the legislature, ending Reconstruction in Mississippi.

trailblazers.name: Pushmataha
trailblazers.text: One of three regional chiefs of the Choctaw, known for his skill in war and diplomacy. He turned down Tecumseh's call to join an alliance, led Choctaw fighters on the side of the United States in the War of 1812, and negotiated several treaties with the United States.

trailblazers.name: Elizabeth Taylor Greenfield
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery in Natchez, she was taken to Philadelphia as a child by her enslaver, Elizabeth Holiday Greenfield. She became a concert singer known as "the Black Swan," making her debut in Buffalo, New York, in 1851, and on May 10, 1854, she sang for Queen Victoria at Buckingham Palace.

trailblazers.name: Hiram Revels
trailblazers.text: A minister born free in North Carolina, he helped organize Black Union regiments during the Civil War. In 1870 the Mississippi legislature elected him to the U.S. Senate, making him the first African American in Congress, and he then became the first president of Alcorn Agricultural and Mechanical College (now Alcorn State University).

trailblazers.name: Ida B. Wells
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery in Holly Springs and freed as a baby when Union troops arrived, she became a teacher and investigative journalist. She exposed the truth about lynching in the 1890s and helped found the NAACP.

trailblazers.name: Martha Lum and the Lum family of Rosedale
trailblazers.text: In 1924 nine-year-old Martha Lum, a U.S.-born girl from a Chinese American family in the Mississippi Delta, was barred from Rosedale Consolidated High School in Bolivar County, a school for white students, because she was of Chinese descent. Her father, Gong Lum, took the case to court. On November 21, 1927, in Gong Lum v. Rice, the U.S. Supreme Court used the "separate but equal" rule of Plessy v. Ferguson and ruled 9 to 0 that Mississippi could classify her as "colored" and require her to attend a school for Black children.

trailblazers.name: Medgar Evers
trailblazers.text: A World War II veteran, he became the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi. He worked to end segregation, including at the University of Mississippi, and to protect voting rights, and he was murdered in 1963 for this work.

trailblazers.name: Fannie Lou Hamer
trailblazers.text: She was threatened, shot at, and beaten for trying to register to vote, yet she helped thousands of Black Mississippians register. She was vice-chair of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party at the 1964 Democratic National Convention and started the Freedom Farm Cooperative.

landforms: Pine Hills and North Central Hills
Pontotoc Ridge and Fall Line Hills
waters: Sardis Lake and Ross Barnett Reservoir
geography.regions: Almost all of Mississippi lies on the low hills and plains of the East Gulf Coastal Plain, with the flat, fertile Delta in the northwest and the Gulf Coast in the south.

ecosystems.name: Longleaf pine forests and bogs
ecosystems.about: Longleaf pine covers much of the southeast, along with pitcher plant (Sarracenia) bogs. Over half of Mississippi is covered by trees.

ecosystems.name: Delta bottomland forests
ecosystems.about: The Delta is mostly farmland and fish ponds today but still has large stands of bald cypress, cottonwood, willow, and oak.

ecosystems.name: Rivers and streams
ecosystems.about: Mississippi's rivers hold about 90 species of native freshwater mussels.

ecosystems.name: Black Belt and Jackson prairies
ecosystems.about: Two bands of prairie with dark, fertile soil cross the middle and northeast of the state, though most has been turned into farms.

science.weather: Hot, humid summers and mild winters (humid subtropical). Hurricanes from the Gulf of Mexico are the biggest danger: Hurricane Camille (1969) and Hurricane Katrina (2005, which killed 238 people in the state) caused huge storm surge damage. The state averages about 27 tornadoes a year.
science.resources: Agriculture and forestry are major industries: Mississippi raises more than half of the nation's farm-raised catfish and is a top producer of sweet potatoes, cotton, and pulpwood. Manufacturing, transportation, and health services are also important.
science.highlight: The state fossil is a prehistoric whale. Basilosaurus lived about 41 to 34 million years ago, grew up to about 66 feet long, and hunted in a shallow sea; scientists first thought its bones belonged to a giant reptile.

g3_ss.title: Mississippi Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Jackson, the Delta, and the Gulf Coast, and learn what the Legislature, governor, and Supreme Court do.

g3_ss.title: Mississippi's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Learn about the Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Natchez, the mound builders, and the Mississippi Band of Choctaw today.

g3_ss.title: Mississippi Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Hiram Revels, Ida B. Wells, Medgar Evers, and Fannie Lou Hamer and how each stood up for fairness.

g45_ss.title: Mississippi's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study Emerald Mound, the Grand Village of the Natchez, Nanih Waiya, and Choctaw and Chickasaw homelands.

g45_ss.title: Colonies, Cotton, and Removal
g45_ss.plan: Trace French settlement, the Natchez War, slavery and cotton, and the Treaties of Dancing Rabbit Creek and Pontotoc Creek.

g45_ss.title: Mississippi 1817–1877
g45_ss.plan: Examine statehood, slavery, the Civil War and Vicksburg, the 1868 convention and Hiram Revels, and the violent end of Reconstruction in 1875.

g3_sci.title: Hurricanes on the Gulf Coast
g3_sci.plan: Learn how hurricanes form over the Gulf and how storm surge works, using Katrina as an example.

g3_sci.title: The Mighty Mississippi
g3_sci.plan: Explore the river, the Delta, and the plants and animals of bottomland forests.

g3_sci.title: Pine Forests and Pitcher Plants
g3_sci.plan: Meet longleaf pines and the carnivorous pitcher plants of Mississippi bogs.

g45_sci.title: Ancient Whales of Mississippi
g45_sci.plan: Use the state fossil Basilosaurus to study how fossils show that a sea once covered the region.

g45_sci.title: Soil, Farming, and Catfish
g45_sci.plan: Investigate Delta soil and loess, crops, and why fish farming is big in Mississippi.

g45_sci.title: Tornadoes and Severe Weather
g45_sci.plan: Graph Mississippi tornado data and learn how storms form and how to stay safe.
